mainEntity.name: What's the difference between perimenopause and menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Perimenopause is the transition phase leading up to menopause when hormone levels begin fluctuating. Menopause officially begins after 12 consecutive months without a menstrual cycle.

mainEntity.name: What are the early signs of perimenopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Early symptoms may include irregular periods, mood changes, fatigue, sleep issues, brain fog, low libido, and hot flashes.

mainEntity.name: When should I consider hormone therapy?

acceptedAnswer.text: If symptoms are affecting your quality of life, daily routine, sleep, relationships, or energy levels, it may be time to consider a medical evaluation and discuss hormone therapy options.

mainEntity.name: Can perimenopause cause weight gain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Hormonal changes can affect metabolism, muscle mass, insulin sensitivity, and fat storage, making weight management more difficult.

mainEntity.name: Is hormone therapy safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hormone therapy may be safe and effective for many women when carefully monitored by a qualified medical provider. Treatment plans should always be personalized based on medical history, symptoms, and labwork.

mainEntity.name: Do I need lab testing before treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Comprehensive lab testing helps us understand hormone levels, thyroid function, metabolic health, and other important markers before creating a treatment plan.

mainEntity.name: How long does treatment take to work?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some women notice improvements within weeks, while others may need more time and ongoing adjustments depending on their symptoms and treatment plan.

mainEntity.name: What causes changes in sexual health for women?

acceptedAnswer.text: Changes in female sexual wellness are often related to hormonal shifts, aging, childbirth, or menopause. These changes can affect vaginal tissue, lubrication, sensitivity, and overall comfort during intimacy. Treatments such as hormone therapy, laser vaginal rejuvenation, and PRP can help restore tissue health and sexual responsiveness.

mainEntity.name: Can vaginal rejuvenation help with dryness or discomfort?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Treatments like CO2 laser therapy help stimulate collagen production in vaginal tissue, which can improve lubrication, elasticity, and overall tissue health. Many women notice reduced dryness and increased comfort during intimacy after treatment.

mainEntity.name: What is the Plasma Shot (PRP therapy) for women?

acceptedAnswer.text: PRP therapy, often referred to as the O-Shot, uses platelet-rich plasma from your own blood to stimulate tissue regeneration and improve circulation in areas involved in sexual response. This may help improve sensitivity, arousal, and orgasm quality for some women.

mainEntity.name: Can these treatments help after menopause?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Many women seek treatment during or after menopause when hormonal changes lead to vaginal dryness, thinning tissue, and reduced libido. Treatments such as hormone therapy, PRP, and laser therapy can help restore comfort and sexual wellness.

mainEntity.name: Is there downtime after treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most treatments require little to no downtime. PRP treatments typically allow patients to resume normal activities immediately, while laser treatments may involve mild sensitivity or discharge for a short period.

mainEntity.name: How many treatments are usually needed?

acceptedAnswer.text: The number of treatments depends on the therapy used and the patient's individual goals. Some PRP treatments may show results after one session, while laser therapy is often performed as a series of treatments followed by occasional maintenance.

mainEntity.name: Is vaginal rejuvenation safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vaginal rejuvenation treatments performed by trained medical professionals are generally safe and minimally invasive. At Savannah Age Management Medicine, all therapies are performed under medical supervision using established treatment protocols.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between standard dosing and microdosing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Standard dosing follows a manufacturer's "escalation" schedule aimed at maximum weight loss. Microdosing uses significantly smaller amounts to achieve metabolic "quiet" and health benefits without the "food aversion" or GI distress.

mainEntity.name: Will I still lose weight?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, but the focus is on quality weight loss. By losing weight more gradually at a lower dose, you are much more likely to preserve muscle mass and maintain your metabolic rate.

mainEntity.name: Can I do this if I'm already on Hormone Replacement Therapy (BHRT)?

acceptedAnswer.text: Absolutely. In fact, many patients find that microdosing GLP-1s is the "missing piece" that helps their BHRT work more effectively by fixing underlying insulin resistance.

mainEntity.name: How do I know what my "microdose" is?

acceptedAnswer.text: That is where our expertise comes in. We start low and use your feedback—and your lab data—to find the exact level where your cravings vanish and your energy peaks.

Bioidentical Hormone Replacement Therapy (BHRT)
jsonLd.description: Bioidentical Hormone Replacement Therapy (BHRT) for men and women is a specialty at Savannah Age Management Medicine. Each patient is assessed individually based on lab values and reported symptoms. Learn more about the BHRT program from Medical Director Harry Collins, DO, FACOG, and John Kurtz, PA, MPAS.

mainEntity.name: What is BHRT?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bioidentical Hormone Replacement Therapy (BHRT) uses hormones that are chemically identical to the ones your body naturally produces. It is designed to restore balance and relieve symptoms of hormone deficiencies or imbalances, particularly during aging, menopause, or andropause.

mainEntity.name: Differences between BHRT, HRT, and TRT

acceptedAnswer.text: BHRT is the most comprehensive way to treat dysregulated hormone levels in both men and women. Click the link below for more information on the differences between these treatment methods.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I need BHRT?

acceptedAnswer.text: Signs that males and females might need BHRT: Fatigue or energy loss, Loss of libido or arousal response, Irregular menstrual cycles, Hot flashes or night sweats, Mood changes or fluctuation, Memory issues, Weight gain, Sleep problems, Muscle loss.

mainEntity.name: How is BHRT different from traditional hormone therapy?

acceptedAnswer.text: BHRT hormones match your body's natural hormones exactly. Our program is designed to tailor dosing precisely to your levels, symptoms, and needs. For more even and sustained results, our program leverages injections rather than pellets.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to see results?

acceptedAnswer.text: Patients will begin to experience initial improvements in the first 2-3 weeks, with full benefits within 3-6 months. Regular monitoring and adjustment of medication levels may be required.

mainEntity.name: What benefits can I expect from treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Benefits of BHRT include but are not limited to: Improved energy levels, Better sleep quality, Enhanced mood stability, Increased mental clarity, Improved libido, Better muscle tone, Reduced hot flashes, More stable weight management.

mainEntity.name: Are hormone medications, lab work, and appointments included?

acceptedAnswer.text: Patient cost includes appointment and assessment time, fitness evaluation and recommendation, body composition scans, nutritional guidance, in-office lab draws, quick care, and access to Fullscript supplements. The cost of labs and medications are up to the patient, or can be billed through insurance. Most insurance companies will cover the cost of lab work, but may not cover the cost of hormone medications. Please note that we do have a partnership with PatientFi to help make payments easier.

mainEntity.name: Do you offer pellets?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. In our experience, pellets are invasive, difficult to manage, and do not evenly deliver hormones.

mainEntity.name: Can your office serve as my Primary Care Physician?

acceptedAnswer.text: We can offer Quick Care for things such as a sinus infection, COVID, Urinary Tract Infection,etc. However, we recommend you maintain a relationship with a Primary Care Physician or specialist for any chronic conditions you may have.

mainEntity.name: Will you refill medications that I am currently taking from my other physicians such as blood pressure medication, cholesterol medication, heart medication, etc.

acceptedAnswer.text: No. These are medications for chronic conditions that should be managed with your specialist or Primary Care Physician.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to come into the office every week to get my testosterone injections?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. We will teach you how to administer these medications on your own at home.

mainEntity.name: What if I need to see one of your providers during the year? Will I be able to make an appointment and be seen or will this be an extra fee?

acceptedAnswer.text: Within reason, our providers will make themselves available to see you during the year if you have questions on your progress or treatment protocol. Additional services outside of the scope of BHRT can be administered for a fee.

mainEntity.name: Once I become a BHRT patient, do I receive a discount off of any of the other additional services that you offer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Active BHRT patients will receive 10% of all other services offered in the clinic.

mainEntity.name: Is shockwave therapy for ED painful?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most men describe the sensation as mild tapping or tingling. The device is applied externally and only topical anesthesia is required. Treatment sessions typically last 20 to 30 minutes, and most men resume normal activity the same day.

mainEntity.name: How many shockwave therapy sessions will I need?

acceptedAnswer.text: A standard protocol consists of six sessions, typically spaced one week apart. Some men notice changes during the course of treatment; any improvements often continue to develop over six to twelve weeks as tissue responds. Periodic maintenance sessions may be recommended based on individual results.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between shockwave therapy and acoustic wave therapy?

acceptedAnswer.text: The terms are often used interchangeably and refer to the same general category of low-intensity sound wave treatment. At SAMM, we use a professional-grade acoustic wave device to deliver targeted therapy — the same mechanism studied in clinical research on low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy (LI-ESWT) for ED.

mainEntity.name: Is shockwave therapy for ED FDA approved?

acceptedAnswer.text: Shockwave therapy for erectile dysfunction is currently considered an emerging treatment option in the United States. While low-intensity shockwave therapy has FDA-cleared devices and is supported by leading European urology guidelines, it is classified as investigational by the American Urological Association, meaning clinical evidence continues to evolve. We discuss the current research and realistic expectations with every patient during consultation.

mainEntity.name: Can shockwave therapy help if pills are less effective?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some men who have experienced reduced effectiveness with PDE5 inhibitors have reported improvement following a course of shockwave treatment, potentially due to enhanced vascular function. Results vary by individual, and this is discussed in detail at your consultation.

mainEntity.name: Who performs shockwave therapy at SAMM?

acceptedAnswer.text: All shockwave therapy treatments at Savannah Age Management Medicine are performed by our licensed physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant in a private, clinical setting. You will receive a thorough consultation and health history review before any treatment is scheduled.

mainEntity.name: Is shockwave therapy for ED covered by insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Shockwave therapy for erectile dysfunction is typically not covered by insurance and is considered an elective procedure. Pricing and payment options are reviewed in full during your consultation with our team.

openGraph.title: Vitamin D, K2 & Hormone Health  Why Labs Matter

jsonLd.name: Savannah Age Management Medicine - Health & Wellness

mainEntity.name: Do vitamin D3 and K2 help with hormones?

acceptedAnswer.text: They may support systems involved in hormone function, but they are not direct hormone treatments. Their role depends on your overall clinical picture.

mainEntity.name: Does vitamin D boost estrogen?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vitamin D does not directly “boost” estrogen. It may influence broader regulatory pathways, but hormone levels are controlled through more complex mechanisms.

mainEntity.name: Why am I gaining weight despite diet and exercise?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hormonal changes during perimenopause can make weight management more difficult despite healthy habits.

mainEntity.name: Does a regular blood test show vitamin D?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Vitamin D is commonly measured through a 25-hydroxy vitamin D blood test.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between vitamins D and K2?

acceptedAnswer.text: Vitamin D helps regulate calcium absorption. Vitamin K2 helps direct where calcium goes in the body.

mainEntity.name: Can low vitamin D affect how you feel?

acceptedAnswer.text: Low levels may be associated with symptoms like fatigue or low energy, but these symptoms are not specific and require broader evaluation.

mainEntity.name: Should I take vitamin D and K2 together?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Whether either is recommended depends on labwork and clinical context.

mainEntity.name: Can supplements fix a hormone imbalance?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Hormone imbalances typically involve multiple systems and require a comprehensive approach, not a single supplement.

mainEntity.name: Why did my provider check vitamin D during hormone testing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because nutrient status can provide additional context about metabolic and overall health, which may influence symptoms and treatment planning.

itemListElement.name: Semaglutide Vs Tirzepatide For Weight Loss How Clinicians Decide

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between semaglutide and tirzepatide?

acceptedAnswer.text: Semaglutide targets GLP-1 receptors, while tirzepatide targets both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. This difference influences metabolic signaling and treatment selection.

mainEntity.name: Is tirzepatide stronger than semaglutide?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Clinical effectiveness depends on individual metabolic response and tolerance rather than a simple potency comparison.

mainEntity.name: Which medication causes more weight loss?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some patients experience greater weight loss with one therapy than with the other, but outcomes vary widely.

mainEntity.name: Can non-diabetics use semaglutide or tirzepatide?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, these medications may be prescribed for weight management in non-diabetic patients when clinically appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Are semaglutide and tirzepatide safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: When prescribed and monitored by a clinician, both therapies can be used safely in appropriate candidates.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I stop taking a GLP-1 medication?

acceptedAnswer.text: Appetite and metabolic patterns may return to baseline. Lifestyle strategies are essential to maintain results.

mainEntity.name: How do clinicians decide which medication to prescribe?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decisions are based on symptom review, lab results, metabolic markers, body composition data, and treatment goals.

mainEntity.name: Do I need medical supervision while using these medications?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Regular monitoring helps manage side effects and ensures treatment remains aligned with your health needs.

openGraph.title: Can Low Testosterone Cause Erectile Dysfunction?  SAMM

jsonLd.name: Savannah Age Management Medicine - Health & Wellness

mainEntity.name: Can low testosterone cause erectile dysfunction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Low testosterone can contribute to ED, especially through reduced libido and impaired sexual response, but it is not the most common cause.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if ED is hormonal or circulatory?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hormonal ED often presents with low libido first. Circulatory ED is more common and involves blood flow limitations, often tied to metabolic or cardiovascular factors.

mainEntity.name: What testosterone level affects erections?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single cutoff that predicts ED. Symptoms, clinical context, and lab results matter more than a single number.

mainEntity.name: Does treating low testosterone fix ED?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sometimes, if low testosterone is truly contributing. But many men have ED from vascular, psychological, or medication-related causes, so treatment depends on the full evaluation.

mainEntity.name: When should I get tested for ED?

acceptedAnswer.text: If ED persists, affects quality of life, or occurs alongside low libido or risk factors like obesity, diabetes, or sleep issues, testing is appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Can weight, sleep, or stress cause ED?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Metabolic health, poor sleep, and chronic stress are major contributors, especially in younger men.

mainEntity.name: What happens after an ED evaluation?

acceptedAnswer.text: A clinician reviews symptoms, risk factors, hormone labs, and broader health contributors, then discusses appropriate treatment options based on cause.

itemListElement.name: Low Testosterone Symptoms For Men In Their 40s

mainEntity.name: What are the most common symptoms of low testosterone in men?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most common include low libido, erectile changes, fatigue, low motivation, depressed mood, increased body fat, and reduced muscle mass. Symptoms often cluster rather than appearing in isolation.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if it's stress or low testosterone?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can't reliably tell by symptoms alone. Stress, sleep deprivation, and hormone imbalance overlap heavily. Proper testing and clinician review are the only ways to differentiate.

mainEntity.name: What testosterone level is considered low?

acceptedAnswer.text: This is determined on an individual basis. Symptoms and overall clinical symptoms are taken into consideration.

mainEntity.name: When should men get tested?

acceptedAnswer.text: If symptoms persist, affect quality of life, or are accompanied by risk factors like obesity, diabetes, or sleep apnea, testing is reasonable, regardless of age.

mainEntity.name: How is low testosterone diagnosed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Through a combination of symptom assessment, medical history, physical exam, and bloodwork. Diagnosis is never based solely on labs.

mainEntity.name: Can weight and sleep affect testosterone?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Obesity, poor sleep, and sleep apnea are strongly associated with lower testosterone levels.

mainEntity.name: What happens after a low testosterone diagnosis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Your clinician will review options, which may include lifestyle changes, addressing underlying conditions, and potentially hormone therapy. Treatment is individualized.

mainEntity.name: Is treatment safe?

acceptedAnswer.text: When properly prescribed and monitored by a clinician, hormone therapy can be used safely. That's why evaluation and ongoing follow-up are essential.
